passage: Tanvir's village had one good internet spot near the water tank, and that's where he sat with his cousin Binita, typing questions into an AI chat tool for his Class 10 project on local crops. "Ask it to write the whole thing," Binita whispered. It was tempting. The answer came back fast, neat, and full of facts, including a citation to a government report. Tanvir frowned. "It says millets grow best in flooded fields. That's wrong. Abba grows them on the dry side." They tried to find the report. It didn't exist. Binita's grin faded. Tanvir used the tool to make a list of questions instead, then walked to the farm office to ask the officer himself. His project was shorter, but every line was his own.

passage: Kwame had an essay due on the history of the Gold Coast, and it was nearly midnight in Accra. His sister Esther, home from university, found him with an AI tool open and a finished essay on the screen. "You wrote that in ten minutes?" she asked. He shrugged, a bit guilty. "Read me the second paragraph." He did. "Who's that historian?" she asked. He checked. The name led nowhere. "And that date is wrong. I did this for my exams." Kwame groaned. "So I have to start again?" "Use it to explain what confuses you," Esther said. "Then check the facts in your textbook and write it yourself." He grumbled, but by one o'clock he had a messy, honest first draft.

passage: In the Class 12 computer lab, the teacher allowed AI tools for one hour of project work, with a rule: every fact had to be checked against a second source. Jaya asked hers to summarise a chapter on climate. Her friend Ankita asked hers for five references. Ankita was done in five minutes and grinning. Jaya was still reading. "Just copy it," Ankita said. Jaya shook her head and clicked the first reference. It took her to a real journal, but the article said something different. The second link didn't open at all. Ankita checked hers and went quiet; two of her five were made up. She sighed. "So it lies?" "It guesses," Jaya said. "Confidently." They spent the rest of the hour hunting for real sources.

qa.a: Every fact had to be checked against a second source.

qa.a: It suggests she was surprised and a bit uneasy to find two made-up references after feeling confident she was done.

qa.a: It forced students to verify claims, which exposed the made-up and misquoted references before they could spoil the projects.

qa.a: Jaya likely sees it as risky, since every fact had to be checked, so she keeps reading and clicks the first reference instead.

grounding: It shows teens in a school lab finding that AI-generated references can be false and must be checked.

I'm Maria. I sit next to Hafsa in history. Last week we had to write an essay on the salt march.
I saw Hafsa type the question into an AI tool. It gave her a smooth paragraph and a list of four books. I thought she'd just copy it.
Instead she opened the school library's catalogue and searched for each book. Two didn't exist. She showed me. “It made them up. The titles sound real.”
Then she closed the tool and wrote her own essay from our textbook and one real book from the list. She used the AI only to ask it questions and check if she understood.
Her essay was shorter than mine. She got a better mark.

Week one: Simran, fifteen, handed in an essay on photosynthesis written almost entirely by an AI tool. It was polished. Ms Sarita asked her to explain one paragraph aloud. Simran couldn't. Her face burned.
Week two: Simran tried something else. She read the chapter first, then asked the AI to quiz her with ten questions. She got four wrong. She went back to the book for those.
Week four: For the next essay, she wrote her own draft, then asked the AI to point out gaps. It suggested a fact about chlorophyll; she checked it in the textbook, and it was right. Another suggestion was wrong, and she crossed it out.
This time, when Ms Sarita asked her to explain, she did, without notes.

Tushar, you're using that AI to write your project? Let your Harish Chacha tell you about my worst week at work.
I was twenty-six, a junior analyst. My manager asked for a report on water use in factories, due Friday. I was tired. I asked an AI tool to write the background section. It gave me perfect paragraphs, with three research papers cited.
I nearly sent it to the client. At the last minute, my manager, Mrs Rao, asked where one paper came from. I searched. It didn't exist. None of the three did.
I sat in the toilet for ten minutes, feeling sick. Then I rewrote the section myself, with real sources, and stayed till midnight.
Since then, I check every claim, Tushar. Every single one.

qa.a: Checking the source when Mrs Rao asked, then rewriting with real sources; he learned to verify every claim.

In the Kolkata school library, Sharmila watched Disha paste AI answers into her biology worksheet.
"Aren't you going to read it?"
"Why? It's right."
Sharmila pointed at one line. "It says plants take in oxygen for photosynthesis. That's backwards."
Disha frowned. "Oh."
"The tool is good for explaining, but you have to check. And if you just copy, you won't know it in the exam."
Disha sighed. "Okay. What do you do?"
"I ask it to explain a topic like I'm twelve. Then I close it, and write the answer myself. Then I check with the book."
Disha tried it. It took longer. But afterwards she could explain photosynthesis without looking.

Biology teacher's note, Class 10B (Sunaina Ma'am)
I told the class they could use AI tools to understand topics, as long as they wrote their answers themselves and checked the facts.
Zeenat showed me something interesting today. She had asked a chatbot to explain photosynthesis in simple steps. It was helpful, but it said plants give out oxygen "only at night". She frowned at that, checked her textbook and our lab notes, and found it was wrong.
She wrote her own explanation, then put a small note at the bottom: "AI helped explain steps; night claim was wrong, corrected from textbook, p. 84."
I asked her permission and shared her note with the class as an example. Next week I'm going to give everyone an AI answer with two hidden errors to find.

qa.a: It suggests Zeenat felt doubtful and suspicious, sensing the claim didn't fit what she already knew.

qa.q: How could Sunaina Ma'am's error-hunting task help the class?
qa.a: It would train everyone to treat AI answers as drafts to check, not facts to copy.

qa.a: They might feel surprised that an AI can be confidently wrong and realise checking is part of using it honestly.
